claims.text: Adding a short intermediate-temperature dwell during cooling increases atomic diffusion relative to immediate quenching.
Rapid heating and quenching kinetically trap the nanoparticles because there is insufficient atomic diffusion.
The initial rapid-cycle nanoparticles typically exhibit phase separation and elemental segregation.
The initial rapid-cycle nanoparticles typically have uncontrolled particle morphology.
Dwell-enhanced diffusion promotes local atomic reordering and compositional homogenization.
Dwell-enhanced diffusion relieves chemical-potential gradients that would otherwise drive segregation and phase separation.
Increasing the time available for diffusion overcomes kinetic trapping and reduces elemental segregation and phase separation.
The balance between finite diffusion time and the thermodynamic drive associated with high entropy dictates the final crystal structure.
The dwell favors formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Compared with rapid quenching, the dwell will produce fewer secondary phases and less elemental segregation.
Compared with rapid quenching, the dwell will produce more controlled and uniform particle morphology.
The hypothesis applies to compositions containing more than five elements whose atomic-size differences and mixing enthalpies permit entropic stabilization.
The dwell temperature must remain below the onset of thermal decomposition while remaining high enough for appreciable atomic mobility.
Keeping the dwell short prevents excessive grain coarsening and unwanted phase transformations.
Surface segregation involving Au or Cu may respond differently or uncertainly to the dwell intervention.

Failure of the dwell to significantly reduce segregation and phase separation, or worsening of morphology or decomposition relative to the rapid-quench control, would falsify the proposed dwell mechanism.
